data.body:
## Learn to think together

**Grade 6 · With a teacher and a partner · Two short sessions**

Your ideas can help your partner notice something new. Together, work out which reasons support a recommendation.

**Goal:** Explain a reason, respond to another idea, and decide together. The reading corner gives us something to discuss.

**Make:** one shared decision record, built as you go; each person answers three short exit prompts. Follow the four core resources; other activities are optional.

**Warm-up (2 minutes):** Think of a time someone else’s idea changed your mind, or helped you explain your own idea better. Share it with your partner in any way you like, or just keep it in mind.

### The case

Recommend equipment and a routine for a school reading corner, spending **at most 6 equipment tokens**. Open **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** for the facts (Evidence A–E), the prices and two starting plans. Keep it open during the whole lesson.

### Our route

1. **Prepare.** Read the Case Sheet, take quiet thinking time, and choose an idea and supporting fact. Begin row 1 of **Our Shared Decision Record**, or keep brief notes in your usual format. A **proposal** is an idea to consider; **evidence** is information used to support or question an idea; here, use the case facts.
2. **Notice and try.** Use **One Move to Try: Explain and Respond**. Notice the model, then exchange your own ideas and reasons.
3. **Get feedback and retry.** Keep a brief note of the exchange in row 2. Ask for one action to make your reason or response clearer. Try it and receive another reply; add what happened.
4. **Decide.** Finish rows 3–4 of **Our Shared Decision Record**. One person writes; both check that it says what you meant. Include two case facts, the total, and a remaining check. A **tradeoff** is a benefit alongside something left unsolved.
5. **Reflect.** Each person answers the three short prompts in **My Reason and My Response**. The core lesson is complete.

Use speech, writing, typing, signing, a communication board or device (AAC), or a labeled sketch. Keep familiar tools and thinking time; a recorder can help.

**Find an activity again:** Select its title in your resources list. On a small screen, open **My Resources** to find that list.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). This is an original AlloFlow lesson; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

## Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision

**Use with every activity in this pack.** Keep this sheet open while you work.

### The fictional case

Recommend equipment and a routine for a school reading corner. Spend **at most 6 equipment tokens**. All facts and prices are invented. A teacher must check furniture fit and shelf access before any real change.

**Evidence A: Preferences.** In a fictional class of 30, 24 selected a quiet place for independent reading and 18 selected a place to discuss a book with a partner. They could select both choices, so do not add the counts to find a class total.

**Evidence B: A space check.** In the trial layout, a large fixed table blocked the route to one shelf. Any new plan must keep a clear route to every shelf. The teacher will check the actual layout before use.

**Evidence C: A sound check.** During three practice sessions, partner talk could be heard across this small corner. No one has tested whether a divider would reduce that sound.

**Evidence D: A light check.** The existing corner light does not reach every reading position. The room already has another well-lit reading area.

**Evidence E: Available equipment.** A divider costs 3 tokens; a task lamp costs 2; a movable table costs 3; a book basket costs 1; a set of seat pads costs 2. Choose each item at most once. A divider can mark two areas but is not guaranteed to block sound. A movable table can be repositioned; its fit must be checked. A basket can bring books closer; it must not block the route. Seat pads add floor-seating choices, but floor seating is optional. A lamp adds light at one position; check cords and placement before use.

### Two ideas to start with

- **Plan 1:** a lamp (2) and book basket (1): **3 tokens**. Add a schedule for quiet reading and partner discussion. This adds light at one position; it does not light every seat.
- **Plan 2:** a divider (3) and book basket (1): **4 tokens**. Add the same schedule. This marks two areas; it does not prove that sound is blocked.

Compare these starting ideas. You may keep or change them within the budget. If you agree immediately, compare your reasons and one concern.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). ## One move to try: explain and respond

**First, notice this fictional model with your teacher.** Two partners are comparing ideas for a reading corner. Either person could communicate in any familiar way.

Keep **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** open for the facts and prices.

**An exchange that stops too soon**

**Partner 1:** “Choose the divider. It will make the corner silent.”

**Partner 2:** “What about the light?”

**Partner 1:** “I already decided.”

Which idea was left unexplored? Which claim goes beyond the case?

**An exchange that uses another idea**

**Partner 1:** “I propose a divider to mark two areas. The class wants places for quiet reading and partner discussion.”

**Partner 2:** “I propose a lamp. Some reading positions need more light. We could use a schedule for the two activities.”

**Partner 1:** “Do you mean a lamp plus a schedule, instead of expecting a divider to stop sound?”

**Partner 2:** “Yes. One lamp still will not light every seat.”

**Partner 1:** “That helps me compare. The case has not tested whether a divider blocks sound. Let’s compare what each plan would help with.”

Point to the message that checks meaning. What did the reply add to the comparison?

### Now try it with a partner

Agree on one action that will help both ideas be understood. Borrow a move below or suggest your own. Keep the shared goal: explain a reason and respond to the meaning of another idea.

1. Prepare your idea and a reason. You can use: **“I propose ____. Evidence ____ matters because ____.”**
2. Receive your partner’s idea. Check its meaning, then respond to its reason. Try: **“Do you mean ____?”** and **“That makes me think ____ because ____.”** Swap who starts so both people can explain and respond.
3. Keep a short note of your exchange in row 2 of **Our Shared Decision Record**. Ask your partner or teacher for **one action** to make the exchange clearer. For example: “Explain how that fact supports the item you chose.”
4. Try again using the feedback, and receive a new reply. You can keep or revise your idea. Add the feedback and retry to row 2; keep the first attempt.

Use your own words or **Make Thinking Available to One Another** for extra cues. Leave time for each message. If you have not received a reply yet, say so and arrange a chance to continue.

**Pausing between sessions?** Keep your starting ideas, first exchange, and feedback. Next time, reread those notes and begin with the retry in step 4.

**Next:** Finish **Our Shared Decision Record**, then each complete **My Reason and My Response**. No other activity is required today.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). This is an original AlloFlow activity; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

history.title: My Reason and My Response

questions.question: Choose one part of your pair’s reading-corner recommendation. Name one case fact and explain how it supports that part.
questions.expectedAnswer: Accept any defensible choice with a relevant case fact and a reason linking the two. For example, the case describes uneven light and says a task lamp adds light at one position; that supports adding a lamp without claiming it lights every seat. This individual response checks reasoning. The shared record separately holds the two evidence references, token total and remaining check. Do not require a particular purchase or exact sentence pattern.

questions.question: What idea did your partner share, and how did you respond to it? If you are still waiting for a reply, say what chance you need to continue.
questions.expectedAnswer: Look for an accurate account of a real contribution and a response to its meaning, such as a question, a check of what the partner meant, or a reason for keeping or changing the plan. Accept an honest report that a reply is still missing, and arrange another exchange. Peer names, agreement, a changed purchase, polished writing or a particular communication method are not required.

questions.question: Name one thing that helped, stayed unclear, or was not useful in your exchange or retry. What will you keep doing or try next time?
questions.expectedAnswer: Accept an honest example tied to the actual exchange or retry: something that helped, stayed unclear, or was not useful. Look for a next action that follows from it. A claim of improvement is not required. Use the response to plan the next opportunity or teaching move.

data.body:
## Later practice: choose one

**Your core lesson is complete after My Reason and My Response.** Use this menu with your teacher when you have a purpose for more practice. Choose one route and a useful way to keep your work.

### Try a clearer exchange

Use **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry** for about 15 minutes, with more time as needed. Choose a message from your own discussion or revisit **One Move to Try: Explain and Respond**. **Pause and Try: Choose a Move** supplies optional picture-supported models. For a sentence cue, choose one from **Make Thinking Available to One Another**; your own wording is welcome.

Prepare a message → receive and respond to a real reply → ask for one feedback action → retry → compare the attempts. Keep brief notes in rows 1–5 of the Practice Record or your usual format. If a reply has not arrived, arrange a chance to continue. **Repair the Exchange** is an alternative analysis of fictional messages with teacher feedback.

### Examine a written record

Open **Read the Record: Reply or Shared Action?** Use two questions:

1. Does the excerpt record a reply that addresses another message’s meaning?
2. Does it record an agreed shared decision or connected next action?

Choose Reply only, Shared action only, Both, or Neither using the words in the excerpt. A private note can be useful even when it records neither. The pictures supply context. Before **Check**, explain one choice and what the excerpt leaves unknown. Then open **Why?** and compare its explanation with yours.

**Keep your reasoning:** placements reset when you close the sort. Keep one brief note while it is open: excerpt, category, supporting words, and remaining question. You can keep that note or copy it into the optional last row of the Practice Record. One explanation is enough.

### Investigate a picture and a message

Use **Picture, Record, Reconsider** with **Evidence Investigator’s Notebook** for about 12 minutes, adjusting as needed. Describe a picture detail, compare it with the separate written record, and name a question. Finish with one sentence about what you kept or reconsidered and why, in Summary or your usual format. Connections is optional. Judge what the records show, rather than how people look.

### Try a routine or a new context

- **Design, Test, and Revise Our Routine:** compare the two illustrated processes, choose or adapt one, try an exchange, and use feedback to decide what to keep.
- **Transfer Lab: What Should We Test Next?:** use a new bridge-data case in a later session. It has its own evidence and uses **Next Round: My Learning Record**.

Keep familiar communication tools, reading support and thinking time in every route.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). These are original AlloFlow activities; Katie Novak did not write or endorse them.

panels.title: Keep a proposal—with reasons
panels.caption:
**Same starting point:** Two partners are choosing a reading-corner plan. Partner 1 proposes a lamp and basket (3 tokens): some reading positions lack light, and a basket can bring books closer. Partner 2 proposes a divider and basket (4 tokens): the class wants quiet reading and partner discussion, and a divider can mark areas. Another well-lit reading area is available. The divider’s effect on sound has not been tested.

**Partner 1 could keep the proposal:** “You want marked areas for both uses, with another lit area available. I still favor the lamp and basket: some reading positions here lack light, and a lamp serves one position. Your idea makes me ask how we will handle both uses. The divider’s sound effect remains untested; cords, placement and shelf routes need checking. What concern have I missed?”

**Compare both:** In each reply, find (1) the partner’s idea it answers, (2) a case fact and why it matters, and (3) something still to check. Both replies are reasonable; neither is the one right answer.

**Try:** Use your own wording to keep, revise, or question a proposal with reasons. Receive and answer a partner’s actual reply. Use **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry** and the loop in **Later Practice: Choose One**. Mark a missing reply “not yet received.” Use your own words, not this example’s.

panels.caption:
**Use during the Feedback step if a model helps.** This comparison supports the existing partner loop; it is not another required activity.

**Case facts for this example:** Some reading positions lack light. A task lamp adds light at one position; a basket brings books closer.

**Supplied first attempt:** “I propose a lamp and basket. My facts are uneven light and books closer to readers.”

**Feedback A:** “Great work!”

**Feedback B:** “You name evidence. Explain how one fact supports an item in your plan.”

**Compare, then try:** What could each note help the learner do? Which gives a specific next action, and which words in the first attempt show why that action fits? Prepare one sentence explaining how one of those facts supports choosing the lamp or basket. Different accurate explanations are possible; keep the first attempt visible.

questions.question: Use the facts and prices in Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision. A message says: “The divider will make the corner silent. Buy it.” Another says: “I’m considering a task lamp because some reading positions need more light.” The first reply is: “That does not matter.” Write a better next message in your own words. It should (1) respond to the lamp idea and (2) check the divider claim against the case. Then explain how your message helps the pair compare plans.
questions.expectedAnswer: Accept multiple repairs. Look for an accurate response to the lighting proposal, a request to clarify or compare it, and recognition that the divider’s sound effect has not been tested. The case describes uneven lighting; one lamp does not solve every position. For example, a response could check whether the partner wants a lamp at one location and ask how both plans address the case. A polite phrase alone, or substituting a preferred purchase without responding to the other idea, is incomplete. Coach the missing move, not the exact wording. Do not grade speech fluency, grammar unrelated to meaning, or use of a communication support.

questions.question: A group member types: “Before choosing the movable table, how will we check the route to every shelf?” The recorder says, “We have already had our turns,” and closes the decision. Name two things the group could do now: (1) one that answers the question, and (2) one that lets the person who asked confirm or correct the group’s answer. How could these change the recommendation?
questions.expectedAnswer: A strong response takes the route question seriously, links it to the blocked shelf route or the need to check the movable table’s fit, and reopens the comparison or records a check needed before use. It also provides response time and a way for the contributor to confirm or correct the group’s interpretation through a workable communication method. Merely granting another turn without using the message, reading it aloud without checking its meaning, or requiring speech is insufficient. A written, typed, signed, AAC, spoken, or labeled-sketch exchange may satisfy the same criteria.

questions.question: Open Pause and Try: Choose a Move and read the two replies, “Keep a proposal—with reasons” and “Revise a proposal—with reasons.” The pictures are optional. For each reply, find (1) the partner’s idea it answers, (2) a case fact and the reason it matters, and (3) something still to check.
questions.expectedAnswer: Both replies accurately receive the area-marking proposal and the existence of another well-lit area. Reply 1 prioritizes adding light within this corner using the uneven light and one-position lamp facts; it retains the original bundle while acknowledging the two uses and unresolved sound, cord, placement, and route checks. Reply 2 gives more weight to marking areas for quiet reading and partner discussion; the partner’s reminder about the other lit area affects its comparison. It retains lighting, route, and sound uncertainties. The other lit area does not establish that everyone’s lighting needs are met, and neither reply establishes quiet, safe placement, the partner’s acceptance, or a group agreement. Both are defensible provisional responses, not proof of a final best plan. Accept other accurate evidence connections and limits.

questions.question: Why does keeping or changing the purchase, by itself, not show that someone responded thoughtfully? Then write your own next message: keep, change or question a proposal, with a reason. (This is practice with examples; a real partner exchange goes in Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry.)
questions.expectedAnswer: Look for the idea that a purchase choice alone does not show whether someone took in and answered another person’s reasoning. The learner’s own message should engage a received idea and connect a reason or useful question to the case. A changed purchase, unchanged purchase, polite wording, or copied script alone is insufficient. Feedback should address meaning, evidence, and honest uncertainty, without requiring a preferred bundle, forced agreement, speech, or fewer access supports.

reflections.text: Optional, after an actual practice exchange: Describe one partner reply. How did you use it in your retry? What changed, or what still needs work? You may leave this blank if you have not practiced. To choose a practice route, open Later Practice: Choose One. The four questions complete this activity; no partner loop is required here.
Optional: What did you notice about a support you used? Name something to keep, change, or try next. You may use your own wording, and needed communication tools and access supports remain available.

data.body:
## Try the moves in a new subject

**Optional science-and-data extension: about 20 minutes after the reading-space practice.** This task has its own evidence and goal. All measurements are invented for this activity. No bridge construction is required.

### The bridge team's decision

A class tested two folded-paper bridge designs. It can repeat three trials of one design before deciding what to show in a demonstration.

**Your shared goal:** Recommend which design to investigate next, explain what you want to find out, and describe how to make the repeated trials useful.

### Bridge evidence

- **Design A:** supported 12, 13, and 12 identical paper clips in its three trials.
- **Design B:** supported 16, 8, and 17 identical paper clips in its three trials.
- **The recorded test conditions:** same paper type and sheet size, same gap between supports, same kind of clip, and a fresh bridge built for each trial. Each design followed its own folding instructions. Clips were added one at a time at the center, allowing 10 seconds after each addition. A recorded load is the greatest number held for that interval before another clip caused collapse.
- **What is missing:** the record does not explain why results varied. Three trials do not establish what will happen every time. Repeating them can add evidence; repetition alone does not explain a cause.

**Optional picture support:** Open **Bridge Lab: Choose a Useful Question**, immediately after these directions, to revisit the six existing results and compare possible questions. Its caption supplies the comparison without requiring the picture. Return here to continue; this support belongs inside the preparation below.

### Prepare, compare, decide

1. **Prepare (3 minutes).** Study both sets of results. Compare two questions: Why did the results vary? What loads occur in three more trials of our chosen design under the recorded conditions? Explain which the planned trials can address directly and what they cannot establish by themselves. Choose A or B and a useful next question, using either question as a starting point or your own wording. Identify two numbers or test details that support your thinking. Prepare a contribution in a useful communication format.
2. **Exchange (6 minutes).** Explain your proposal. Check that you understood a different proposal, then respond to its reason. If everyone chose the same design, compare different reasons or questions about it. If a communication cue helps, choose one from **Make Thinking Available to One Another** or use your own wording. Keep this round’s work in **Next Round: My Learning Record**.
3. **Decide together (6 minutes).** In **Our decision and exchange** in **Next Round: My Learning Record**, keep one recommendation: the design to test next; two evidence references and why they matter; the question to investigate; conditions to keep the same; and an uncertainty the existing record cannot settle. Explain how the planned three trials could help address your question and what would remain unknown. Explain how another contribution affected your reasoning, or why you kept your proposal after considering it; preserve any unresolved concern.
4. **Check your learning (5 minutes).** Use the notebook guidance below. Point to one actual exchange and its effect, or name a next action if that evidence is not yet visible. Allow additional preparation and communication time as needed.

Your group can use text, a labeled sketch, speech, signing, a communication board or device (AAC), or another accessible method. Choose a recorder or keep individual copies of the agreed meaning; let contributors check it. Each learner reflects on their own contribution as well as the group's decision.

### Make a record you can use

Use **Next Round: My Learning Record**. Keep earlier entries and label new notes by activity or round.

- **My next move:** Choose one action you want to try before the exchange.
- **Our routine:** Record how the group will receive ideas and reach a decision.
- **Our decision and exchange:** Keep the recommendation from step 3, then one actual message, the response it received, and its effect. Brief notes or a reference to a shared record are enough. Let contributors check paraphrases; names are unnecessary.
- **Support choice:** Name what helped and what you will keep or change. Needed communication and access supports remain available.

In **Summary**, complete two short checks: “My learning: I can point to ___ / I need another try at ___.” “Our group's learning: Our decision shows ___ / Our next action is ___.” You can record “not yet observed.” If you lacked a meaningful chance to contribute, name the barrier and a change the group could make. You do not have to claim improvement you cannot show.

data.hook:
## Plan your first use

**Audience and purpose:** teacher-facilitated Grade 6 discussion practice, initially in pairs. Learners explain a reason, respond to another idea, and make a shared recommendation. The invented reading corner supplies a common context; no specialist design knowledge is needed.

**Choose a route:** this pack’s four-resource core takes about two 30-minute sessions. The separate **A Decision We Can Explain** unit offers four sessions with a continuing portfolio and three source articles. They reuse the same case. Choose the route that fits your goal; completing both is unnecessary.

### Before learners begin

1. Read the full fictional reading-corner case in **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** and the model exchange. Confirm that learners can access the facts and compare small token totals; read the facts together or provide a calculator without changing the reasoning goal.
2. Arrange partners and how they will receive one another’s messages. Invite learners to choose useful communication methods and one shared discussion agreement. Allow quiet preparation and response time.
3. Choose a recording method. The app notebook stores text; a paper record, teacher-scribed explanation, or another familiar format can serve the same goal. Keep both contributors’ meaning accurate. One device with teacher facilitation can support the pair’s work. Agree how learners will show or share the record and each individual exit response for feedback; saving on a device does not submit work to the teacher. Keep the case available on paper, a display, or a second view while learners record. Begin notebook row 1 during preparation and row 2 during the exchange; no transcript or copied case is needed.
4. Preview the four core resources. Reading the prepared content, viewing embedded images, and using the authored activities require no Gemini key. Optional AI generation or coaching needs a configured connection. An educator can give the feedback in this lesson.

**Session 1:** run the warm-up, then introduce the case and two starter proposals (about 10 minutes), model one move and allow thinking time (8), then exchange ideas and give one feedback action (12).

**Pause point:** keep each pair’s starting ideas, first exchange, and feedback in rows 1–2 or their chosen format.

**Session 2:** reopen those notes and retry (8), finish rows 3–4 (10), share reasoning (5), and complete individual reflection (7). Extend or split these planning estimates for your group. The class does not need to open every resource.

**Why the two starter plans?** Their shared basket and schedule keep the initial comparison focused on lamp versus divider. Both have a benefit and a limit. Learners can propose another plan; finding all possible equipment combinations is not the task.

### How this pack applies UDL

The design follows a core Universal Design for Learning idea: keep the goal firm and make the ways of reaching it flexible. Every learner works toward the same goal: explain a reason with a case fact and respond to what a partner meant. The notes below name barriers learners often meet in discussion and how this pack reduces them, using the three principles of CAST’s UDL Guidelines (version 3.0).

- **Engagement (the why of learning).** Barrier: fear of being wrong or of speaking first. In this pack: an invented case with more than one defensible answer; two starter plans so no one begins from a blank page; keeping a plan with reasons counts as much as changing it; learners help choose the discussion agreement.
- **Representation (the what of learning).** Barrier: reading load, unfamiliar task words, and pictures some learners cannot see. In this pack: every case fact is in the text; every picture has a full caption and description and is optional; task words are defined in context, with an illustrated glossary; two model exchanges show what a useful reply looks like.
- **Action and Expression (the how of learning).** Barrier: discussion that only counts fast spoken turns. In this pack: speech, writing, typing, signing, AAC, sketches or a scribe all count; preparation and response time are built in; sentence starters are optional; the criteria judge the reasoning and the response, not fluency, eye contact or the number of turns.
- **Learner agency.** Learners ask for one feedback action, retry, and reflect on what helped. This self-monitoring is the purpose of the lesson, not an extra to drop when time is short.

**When you adapt:** change the means freely: timing, grouping, recording format and supports. Keep the goal: a reason linked to evidence and a real response to another person’s idea. If a support starts doing the reasoning for the learner, such as a completed frame they copy, it has changed the goal.

### Standards

This lesson addresses the grade 6 Common Core speaking and listening standard for collaborative discussion:

- **SL.6.1:** take part in collaborative discussions, building on others’ ideas and expressing your own clearly. *The whole lesson.*
- **SL.6.1.A:** come prepared and refer to evidence. *Quiet preparation with the Case Sheet.*
- **SL.6.1.B:** follow agreed discussion rules and roles. *The shared agreement and the recorder role.*
- **SL.6.1.C:** ask and answer specific questions that add to the discussion. *The meaning check and the reply to it.*
- **SL.6.1.D:** review key ideas and show understanding of other perspectives by reflecting and paraphrasing. *Paraphrase checks and the exit reflection.*

Any communication method counts as speaking and listening here: writing, typing, signing, AAC or a scribe. The standard describes the thinking, not the channel.
data.directInstruction:
## Model, notice, and agree

Read the two exchanges in **One Move to Try: Explain and Respond**. Ask what happened to the lighting idea in the first exchange and which claim needs evidence. In the second, locate the meaning check and the response it makes possible.

Invite learners to explain the goal in their own words and propose one sign of a useful exchange. Retain the common criteria: a fact connected to a reason, and a response to another idea’s meaning. Together choose one action to try, such as checking a paraphrase before responding. Students can use a sentence prompt, a brief cue, or their own wording.

If needed, define three task words in context: **proposal** = idea to consider; **evidence** = fact we can point to; **tradeoff** = a benefit alongside something left unsolved. The illustrated glossary supports additional discussion vocabulary.

Keep the challenge in explaining and comparing reasons. Reading aloud, signing, AAC, sketches, thinking time, and a scribe can make that reasoning available. Eye contact, response speed, handwriting, or a particular communication method are not criteria.
data.guidedPractice:
## One exchange, one feedback point, another attempt

Each partner prepares an idea and a reason. Receive the other idea, check its meaning, and respond. Swap who starts. A recorder may write, while both contributors confirm or correct the record.

Choose one feedback action from what actually happened:

- **Fact named, link unclear:** “How does that fact support your choice?”
- **Partner’s meaning uncertain:** “Check that part with your partner, then respond to their reason.”
- **Agreement without a comparison:** “Which other idea did you consider, and why do you still recommend this one?”
- **One contribution is missing:** pause for preparation, agree how to receive the message, and invite the other contributor to check its meaning before deciding.

Allow a retry and a new reply. Use row 2 of **Our Shared Decision Record** to keep a brief first-attempt, feedback, and retry note. A different purchase is unnecessary; a clearer reason or a useful question can matter. If an exchange has not happened, arrange a real opportunity before judging it.

### Optional worked recommendation

Use only when learners need a model of the final product: “We propose a lamp and basket: 3 tokens. The case describes uneven light, and a lamp adds light at one position. We propose separate times for quiet reading and partner discussion. The divider idea helped us consider those uses, but the divider’s effect on sound has not been tested. We still need to check shelf routes, cords and placement.”

Other recommendations can be defensible. This is a supplied example, not a learner’s actual exchange or a preferred equipment answer.
data.independentPractice:
## Gather a small amount of useful evidence

Complete the running notebook; do not ask learners to recreate their exchange from memory. Its four rows are starting ideas; exchange and retry; recommendation; remaining check. The recommendation includes two case facts, items and total, and a routine. Brief notes are sufficient.

Each learner then answers the three short prompts in **My Reason and My Response** in any format that works for them. Look for their own fact-to-reason connection and a real response to another contribution. Invite them to identify what helped, remained unclear, or was not useful, and a next action. Accept uncertainty; use it to plan the next opportunity.

### Choose later practice by need

- **More rehearsal:** Practice Record with an optional Pause and Try model. Keep actual replies separate from supplied examples.
- **Interpreting messages:** the record sort. Ask for one placement explained with exact words, then use **Why?** after Check. Categories describe the limited excerpt, not the people.
- **Distinguishing evidence and inference:** Picture, Record, Reconsider with the Investigator’s Notebook. Written records supply the exchanges; appearance alone cannot establish reasoning.
- **More learner ownership:** the routine studio. Compare processes, test one with real messages, and justify keeping or adjusting a step.
- **Transfer to a new context:** the bridge task. Either design can be selected for further investigation with reasons. More trials can add load data; they cannot alone establish why results varied.

The **Later Practice: Choose One** menu supplies the activity directions. These routes are alternatives, not a further checklist.

### Sort reference

Records 1–2: reply only. Records 3–4: agreed shared action only. Records 5–6: both. Records 7–8: neither recorded here. The on-card explanations identify the supporting words. Private preparation can be useful; a planned exchange is not an observed reply, and an agreed plan does not show its implementation.
data.closure:
## Reflect, then decide what to teach next

Ask learners to point to one message, reason, or retry and explain what helped, remained unclear, or was not useful. Choose something to keep or try next. Invite feedback on the prompt or routine itself. A learner may choose different wording or a different useful support. Needed communication and access supports remain available.

### Case facts and practical limits

All case quantities are fictional. The preference counts can overlap. The divider has no measured sound effect; one lamp serves one position. Spend at most six tokens and choose each item at most once. The pictures are not scaled plans. A real teacher would need to check placement, cords and shelf routes before changing a room. Students name a needed check; they do not certify safety or furniture fit.

### Source connection and authorship

[Katie Novak’s Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) is written for educators. It supports explicit modeling, preparation, varied reciprocal communication, shared decision routines, and reflection. This pack connects those ideas to its model, quiet preparation, actual exchange, joint record, and exit reflection.

The case, scripts, grade, timing, criteria, activities and AI-generated cut-paper illustrations are independent AlloFlow authoring choices. They are not Katie’s lesson, rubric, or a tested program. Katie Novak and Novak Education have not authored, reviewed, or endorsed this draft. The companion guide is not reproduced; follow the article for its original context and resources.

**Educator review:** check the examples, responses, access, timing and student navigation with your group before teaching. Classroom effectiveness has not been established by software checks.
